actions.name: Verify patient identity (two identifiers)
actions.result: Patient confirms full name Joyce Mensah and date of birth 03/14/1970; matches registration record. Identity verified per two-identifier policy.

actions.name: Review original specimen collection details from courier/collection log
actions.result: Collection site log: specimen collected 2:10 PM, picked up by courier 4:45 PM, received in lab 7:05 PM (~5 hours post-collection), transported unrefrigerated in delivery van on an 89°F day. Specimen was never centrifuged/separated prior to transport. Log notes draw was described by site staff as 'difficult' but does not detail number of attempts, tourniquet time, or technique used — recommend confirming collection details directly with patient.

actions.name: Review yesterday's critical potassium result and sample flags
actions.result: Potassium 6.3 mmol/L (H, critical; ref 3.5-5.1 mmol/L). Hemolysis index 2+ flagged by analyzer. LDH elevated. Sodium 139 mmol/L (normal), creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (normal), glucose 104 mg/dL (normal).

actions.name: Compare to prior potassium result 3 months ago
actions.result: Potassium 3 months ago: 4.6 mmol/L (normal, no hemolysis flag, routine venous draw, same medication regimen reported at that visit).

actions.name: Assess probability that result reflects true hyperkalemia vs. pre-analytical hemolysis artifact
actions.result: Documented assessment: markedly discordant from baseline, hemolysis index 2+, prolonged tourniquet time with fist pumping, delayed unspun transport in heat, and normal creatinine/sodium together strongly suggest spurious elevation from hemolysis and specimen handling; however patient is on an ACE inhibitor, a potassium-sparing diuretic, and a potassium-based salt substitute, so true hyperkalemia cannot be excluded without a clean recollection.

actions.name: Arrange urgent same-day recollection with special handling instructions
actions.result: Same-day STAT recollection ordered: free-flowing draw, tourniquet released within 1 minute, no fist pumping, immediate gentle inversion, prompt delivery to lab (or walk-in collection site) for processing within 60 minutes, specimen to be centrifuged and separated promptly on arrival; patient scheduled for 2:00 PM today at nearby walk-in draw station.

actions.name: Report critical potassium value to ordering provider per critical-value protocol
actions.result: Critical value 6.3 mmol/L called to ordering provider's office at 9:40 AM; read-back confirmed with on-call nurse; documented time, name of recipient, and that recollection is already arranged. Provider will determine any clinical action pending repeat result.

actions.name: Point-of-care style symptom screen for hyperkalemia (ask patient to report any fatigue, palpitations, weakness, nausea)
actions.result: Patient reports feeling well overall; denies palpitations, muscle weakness, numbness/tingling, nausea, or shortness of breath.

actions.name: Ask about diet and salt substitute use, and check patient's understanding of its contents
actions.result: Patient mentions trying to eat healthier and cut back on salt per her doctor's advice; when asked more specifically about any salt substitutes or seasonings used regularly, she becomes a little hesitant before confirming she uses a 'no-salt' seasoning at most meals. When the learner explains that this type of substitute is typically potassium chloride-based and checks her understanding, she expresses surprise, saying she thought it was just a 'healthier salt' and did not know it contained potassium.

actions.name: Review medication list for other potassium-affecting drugs
actions.result: Current medication list reviewed: lisinopril 20 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily; no NSAIDs, no potassium supplements beyond salt substitute, no trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or other high-risk interacting drugs listed.

actions.name: Instruct patient on fist-clenching avoidance and arm positioning for recollection
actions.result: Patient coached: keep arm relaxed and straight during draw, avoid making a fist or pumping hand, let phlebotomist know if tourniquet feels tight or prolonged, request release of tourniquet as soon as blood flow starts.

actions.name: Confirm patient's current location and ability to reach a draw site same day
actions.result: Patient confirms she is near end of a home-care shift in Worcester and can reach the affiliated walk-in draw site within 2 hours; transportation available via her own car.

actions.name: Determine whether this role should advise changing or holding medications
actions.result: Outside laboratory scope: no instruction given to stop or adjust lisinopril, spironolactone, or salt substitute; patient advised that any medication decisions will come from her prescribing provider after reviewing the repeat result.

artifacts.title: Specimen Handling & Hemolysis Flag Report
artifacts.author: Central Lab Pre-Analytical QA
artifacts.body: Hemolysis index: 2+ (moderate-to-marked hemolysis, visible pink/red tinge in serum). LDH disproportionately elevated relative to other analytes, consistent with in vitro hemolysis (see chemistry panel for value). Specimen type: serum separator tube, received NOT centrifuged. Time from collection to receipt: 5 hours 0 minutes (collected 2:10 PM, received 7:05 PM). Transport condition: ambient temperature, non-refrigerated courier van; outdoor ambient temperature recorded at 89°F at time of transport. Collection site notes: 'Draw described as difficult by collecting staff; patient reported discomfort during procedure.' Specific details of number of attempts, tourniquet duration, and technique were not recorded in this QA report. QA comment: Result flagged for pre-analytical review prior to release; critical value called per protocol pending recollection recommendation.

objectives.text: Verify patient identity using two identifiers before discussing results or arranging recollection.

Identify multiple pre-analytical factors (prolonged tourniquet time, fist pumping, difficult multi-attempt draw, delayed unspun transport in heat, hemolysis index 2+) that can spuriously elevate potassium, and distinguish these from true hyperkalemia risk factors.

Recognize that medications (ACE inhibitor, potassium-sparing diuretic) and potassium-containing salt substitute use raise genuine concern for hyperkalemia, so the abnormal result cannot be dismissed as artifact alone despite strong pre-analytical evidence.
Explain the need for urgent recollection to the patient in plain, reassuring language and arrange a same-day draw with corrected technique.
Report the critical potassium value to the ordering provider per protocol, documenting the call and read-back, while staying within laboratory scope by not advising on medication changes.
Use the three-month-prior potassium trend and today's normal creatinine/sodium to support clinical reasoning about artifact versus true elevation.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Spuriously elevated potassium (pseudohyperkalemia) most likely due to pre-analytical hemolysis and specimen mishandling (prolonged tourniquet time with fist pumping during a difficult multi-attempt draw, plus 5-hour delayed unspun transport in hot conditions), superimposed on a patient with genuine risk factors for true hyperkalemia (ACE inhibitor, potassium-sparing diuretic, potassium chloride salt substitute) that cannot be fully excluded without a clean recollection.
differential: Pre-analytical hemolysis/pseudohyperkalemia from traumatic draw and delayed/unrefrigerated transport
True mild-to-moderate hyperkalemia from combined ACE inhibitor + spironolactone + potassium-based salt substitute
Combination of both: baseline mild true elevation further exaggerated by hemolysis artifact
Laboratory analyzer or specimen labeling error (less likely given clear chain-of-custody and QA documentation)
keyFindings: Potassium 6.3 mmol/L critical, up from 4.6 mmol/L three months ago
Hemolysis index 2+ and elevated LDH flagged on the analyzer
Specimen received 5 hours post-collection, unspun, transported unrefrigerated on an 89°F day
Documented difficult draw: 3 attempts, ~4 minute tourniquet time, instructed fist pumping
Sodium, creatinine, and glucose all normal, arguing against renal failure or severe systemic illness as the cause
Patient on lisinopril and spironolactone, plus regular use of a potassium chloride salt substitute she did not realize contained potassium
Patient asymptomatic: no weakness, palpitations, numbness, nausea, or dyspnea
plan: Arrange urgent same-day recollection using a free-flowing draw technique: minimal tourniquet time (<1 minute), no fist pumping, gentle handling, and rapid transport with prompt centrifugation/separation (within 60 minutes)
Report the critical potassium value to the ordering provider with read-back confirmation, including pre-analytical concerns and recollection plan already in motion
Document pre-analytical investigation findings (collection log, hemolysis index, transport delay) in the laboratory communication record
Do not advise the patient to stop, hold, or adjust lisinopril, spironolactone, or the salt substitute; defer all medication decisions to the ordering provider pending the repeat result

Educate the patient in plain language about why a repeat draw is needed and about the potassium content of her salt substitute, while clarifying that the laboratory cannot provide dietary or medication instructions beyond general education
Flag for follow-up: ensure repeat result reaches the ordering provider promptly and confirm it is reviewed before the end of the day
redFlags: If recollected potassium remains critically elevated, this needs immediate provider notification given patient's ACE inhibitor/spironolactone/salt substitute combination

Any emergence of symptoms (palpitations, weakness, numbness) before recollection should prompt immediate escalation to the ordering provider or emergency care rather than waiting for the scheduled draw
Persistent hemolysis or pre-analytical problems on repeat draw warrant escalation to collection site supervisor for technique review
educationPoints: Prolonged tourniquet application and fist pumping during venipuncture can falsely elevate potassium by promoting local efflux of potassium from muscle and red cells
Hemolysis releases intracellular potassium into serum, and even non-visible hemolysis can be detected by the analyzer's hemolysis index
Delayed, unrefrigerated, unspun transport allows continued cellular metabolism and potassium leakage from blood cells, further elevating measured potassium
Salt substitutes are commonly potassium chloride-based and are an under-recognized contributor to hyperkalemia risk, especially combined with ACE inhibitors and potassium-sparing diuretics
Normal sodium, creatinine, and glucose alongside a markedly abnormal potassium and hemolysis flag should raise suspicion for a pre-analytical artifact rather than acute renal or metabolic failure

Laboratory professionals report critical values to providers and investigate pre-analytical causes, but medication and treatment decisions remain outside their scope and must be deferred to the ordering clinician

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient recalls her last blood test a few months ago was 'normal' and does not initially recognize how different today's critical value is from that baseline.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Chemistry panel from 3 months ago (d3) shows potassium 4.6 mmol/L, clearly normal, while yesterday's result (d1) shows 6.3 mmol/L flagged critical with 2+ hemolysis - a dramatic and inconsistent jump that the patient does not initially appreciate as significant.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may not recognize the clinical significance of a dramatic change between two 'normal-feeling' visits; the learner must use the trend data to explain why this result cannot simply be dismissed as a lab mistake or ignored, while also recognizing the hemolysis evidence as the most likely explanation.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient did not realize her salt substitute contained potassium and considers it just a 'healthier salt' unrelated to her blood test.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list (d4) and clinical reasoning show she is on lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) and spironolactone (potassium-sparing diuretic) with no documented potassium supplement, yet her regular use of a potassium chloride-based salt substitute is a significant unlisted source of dietary potassium intake not captured anywhere in the formal medication list.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Salt substitutes are frequently omitted from medication reconciliation because patients view them as food, not medicine; the learner should recognize this gap and understand why dietary potassium sources must be explored directly rather than relying on the medication list alone.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports a difficult venipuncture yesterday requiring multiple attempts, with the tourniquet left on a long time and being told to pump her fist.
mismatches.recordEvidence: The pre-analytical QA report (d2) only documents that the draw was 'difficult' per collecting staff, without recording number of attempts, tourniquet duration, or fist-pumping instruction - the specific technique details are missing from the formal log and must be obtained directly from the patient.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Collection logs and QA reports do not always capture granular technique details; interviewing the patient directly about her experience of the draw can reveal pre-analytical error sources that are not documented anywhere in the formal record.

patient.name: Joyce Mensah
patient.appearance: A woman in her mid-fifties with a sturdy build, short natural hair pulled back under a patterned headwrap, wearing light blue scrubs from her job. She is seated in what looks like a car parked outside a client's house, late-morning light coming through the windshield, phone propped on the dashboard, occasionally glancing at the time.

persona.personality: Practical, plain-spoken, a little guarded about admitting she skipped details, but warms up with respectful, clear explanation.
persona.communicationStyle: Direct and brief, tends to answer the question asked without elaborating unless prompted; uses everyday language, not medical terms.
persona.emotionalState: Mildly anxious about the word 'critical' but mostly impatient and skeptical since she feels physically fine; softens once she understands the reasoning.
persona.background: Joyce immigrated from Ghana over 20 years ago and has worked as a home health aide in Worcester for the past 12 years, often working back-to-back client shifts with little downtime. She manages her hypertension with medication and tries to eat healthier, including switching to a salt substitute on her doctor's advice about a year ago. She values punctuality and is proud of rarely missing work.
speechExamples: I feel fine, so I don't really understand why I have to come back.
That arm's still a little sore from yesterday, three pokes is a lot.
Wait, that seasoning has potassium in it? Nobody told me that.
If it's quick I can go, but I'm on the clock here.
I take my pills every morning, I don't play around with that.
concerns: Why does she need another needle stick so soon after a difficult draw
Whether something is seriously wrong with her even though she feels well
Fitting a same-day recollection into her tight work schedule
Confusion about why a 'healthy' salt substitute could be a problem

scenario.studentBrief: You are a medical laboratory science student staffing a telehealth laboratory callback line. Joyce Mensah, 55, had routine bloodwork yesterday at a satellite collection site; the lab reported a critical potassium result. You are calling her to verify her identity, investigate possible causes of this result, explain why a repeat draw is needed, arrange urgent same-day recollection, and report the critical value to her ordering provider. Stay within your scope: do not advise on medications or treatment.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Critical potassium result on routine bloodwork, patient feels well and is unsure why a repeat draw is needed.
scenario.openingLine: Hi, yes, this is Joyce. They told me my potassium came back high and I need to come back in? I feel completely fine though, so I'm a little confused.
tasks: Verify the patient's identity using two identifiers before discussing results.
Take a focused history of the blood collection experience and any symptoms.
Review medications and dietary habits with the patient.
Explain in plain language why an urgent same-day recollection is necessary and arrange it with corrected technique instructions.
Report the critical value to the ordering provider per protocol and document the call, while staying within laboratory scope (no medication advice).

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient seated in her parked car outside a client's home during a work break, Worcester, Massachusetts
profile.summary: A 55-year-old home health aide is called back after a critical potassium of 6.3 mmol/L with a 2+ hemolysis flag following a traumatic, delayed blood draw, prompting investigation of pre-analytical causes versus true hyperkalemia risk from her antihypertensive regimen and potassium-based salt substitute. The case teaches MLS students to identify collection and transport errors, weigh them against genuine clinical risk factors, arrange a same-day recollection, and report a critical value to the ordering provider while staying within laboratory scope.
profile.title: Critical Potassium Callback: Hemolyzed, Delayed Specimen in a Patient on ACE Inhibitor, Spironolactone, and a Potassium-Based Salt Substitute
